Arun Bhardwaj Presiding Officer:Motor Accident Claims Tribunalii, Dwarka Courts, New Delhi Mact No. 266/12/10 In The Matter Of : Sh. Baleshwar Munda, S/o Sh. Mitka Munda, R/o Village Bandua, P.O. Baskarcha, P.S. Mahuadar, Distt. Latenhat, Jharkhand. Present address: L & T Labour Colony, Igi Airport, New Delhi. ... Clai Versus 1. Sh. Mahinder Kumar (Driver) S/o Sh. Rajinder Prasad, R/o Flat No. 3, Moti Bagh Market, Smalkha, Kapashera More, Delhi. Permanent R/o Siya Bari Village, P.O. Bourni, P.S. Kafaligair, Distt. Bageshwar, Uttrakhand. 2. M/ s. Jai Chindamani Cranes (Owner) Mothiram Market, Samalkha, Near Kapashera More, New Delhi. Through its Proprietor Sh. K. Rama Prasad, S/o Sh. K. Laxmi, Mact No. 266/12/10 Sh. Baleshwawr Munda v. Sh. Mahinder Kumar & Ors. Page R/o Rzg686, Raj NagarII, Palam Colony, New Delhi. 3. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. (Insurer) D.O. 19, Savitri ChamberII, D13, Local Shopping Complex, Prashant Vihar, Delhi110085. Present Address vs Sh. Respondents Filed On : 11.05.2010 Reserved On : 21.10.2013 Decided On : 29.10.2013 : J U D G M E N T : 1.
texts.facts: This is a claim petition filed under Section 166 and 140 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 for grant of compensation. 2. Respondent no. 1 is the driver, Respondent No. 2 is the owner and Respondent No. 3 is the insurer of the offending vehicle. 3. It is stated in this claim petition that on 20.01.10, at about 7.00 p.m., at L & T Construction Site, Terminal3, IGI Airport, New Delhi, the claimant was working as a helper with his contractor namely Budha Dev Adak. Due to negligent driving of the offending vehicle, a crane bearing temporary no. HR99AX5456 and permanent no. HR55G9229, by Respondent No. 1, the claimant was grievously injured and was treated at Indian Spinal Injuries Centre, Vasant Kunj, New Delhi. 4. It is stated that information of the accident was given at P.S. IGI Airport which was reduced into D.D. Entry No. 23 A dated 20.01.10 and later on it was converted into FIR No. 37/10 registered under Section 279/338 of IPC. 5. It is stated that a sum of Rs. 8,45,000/ is already incurred on the treatment of the claimant. This payment has been given by L & T as per policy of the principal employer and would be deducted from the bills of sub contractor. Therefore, it is prayed that cost of treatment payable to the claimant be given to the sub contractor, Sh. Budha Dev Adak. 6. It is also stated that the claimant was earning Rs. 6,500/ per month and is advised bed rest from the date of accident till the filing of this claim petition. 7. In these circumstances, claimant has claimed a compensation of Rs. 35 lacs from the respondents with interest as applicable from the date of filing of claim petition till its realization. 8. Respondent No. 1 and 2 have filed a common written statement where they have stated that no such accident as alleged in the claim petition has ever taken place due to any rash and negligent driving of Respondent No. 1. Respondent No. 3 had insured the vehicle. Therefore, liability, if any, to pay the compensation is of Respondent No. 3. It is also stated that Respondent No. 1 was having a valid driving license to drive the alleged offending vehicle which was seen by Respondent No. 2 prior to employment of Respondent No. Present Address vs Sh. Mahinder Kumar (Driver) on 29 October, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180513475/ 2 1. Respondent No. 2 had also taken driving test of Respondent No. 1 before employing him as a driver. Therefore, it was denied that there is any responsibility of Respondent No. 1 and 2 to pay any compensation to the claimant. 9. Insurance company stated in its written statement that before any liability could be fastened upon it, the insured must prove that the driver of special type truck bearing no. HR55G9329 was having a valid and effective driving license, permit and fitness on the date of accident. Rest of the contents of claim petition were denied but factum of insurance of the offending vehicle on the date of accident was admitted. OPP 3) Relief. 11. Claimant filed his evidence by way of affidavit stating similar facts as were already stated by him in the claim petition. 12. In cross examination he admitted that the expenses incurred by him on his treatment were directly paid by his principal employer through contractor. Other suggestions contrary to his case were denied by him.
texts.arguments: 13. Claimant examined the Sub Contractor Sh. Budha Dev Adak as PW2 who stated in his evidence by way of affidavit that he is a Sub Contractor with L & T, ECC Division, C/o DIAL at IGI Airport, New Delhi; he is employer of claimant who was working for him as a helper at a salary of Rs. 6,500/ per month; L & T has paid entire cost of medical treatment of claimant which is approximately Rs. 8,50,000/; he was bearing all other expenses of the claimant during treatment period; claimant was admitted for second operation of his head injury in Rockland Hospital and a sum of Rs. 2,38,053/ were spent on his treatment and the expenses incurred by him as well as L & T be given to them by the insurance company of the offending vehicle. 14. In cross examination, he stated that he has a work order given by L & T, the principal employer, but there is no written agreement that expenses incurred by principal employer for the treatment of his employees for injuries suffered by them in the accident while working for principal employer are to be deducted from payments to be given to him by L & T. He admitted that there is no such clause between him and his employer under which he was to pay back expenses incurred on their treatment by him. Other suggestions contrary to his examination in chief were denied by him. Present Address vs Sh. Mahinder Kumar (Driver) on 29 October, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180513475/ 3 15. Sh. M.L. Verma was examined by the claimant as PW3 who stated that he is working as Manager Industrial Relations in DIAL and L & T has spent Rs. 10,96,000/ on the treatment of the claimant. He proved medical bills of the treatment of the claimant as Ex. P1. He stated that L & T has recovered a sum of Rs. 2 lacs from Budha Dev Adak, the Sub Contractor for whom claimant was working at the time of the accident. He further stated that as and when further payments will become due and payable, balance amount will also to be deducted from that contractor. He stated that L & T has a tie up with Indian Spinal Injuries Centre and Rockland Hospital whereby payments are given directly by L & T and L & T recovers it from the contractor whose employee is got treated by L & T. PW3 also stated that there is no written contract in this regard with the contractor. 16. In cross examination, he deposed that claimant was an employee of a sub contractor and he had not brought any documentary evidence with him to show that Rs. 2 lacs were deducted from the account of sub contractor Sh. Budha Dev Adak. He also stated that they did not serve any notice upon the sub contractor stating therein that L & T is incurring expenses on the treatment of his labourer and would be recovering the same from his future bills. 17. This witness was reexamined on the application of the claimant and he stated that sub contractor Sh. Budha Dev Adak is working for L & T since 2006. The sub contractor supplies labour and except for work order, no other agreement is signed between L & T and the sub contractor. He produced the work order as Ex. PW3/3. He stated that the limit of quantum of work which can be assigned to the sub contractor is mentioned in work order which is Rs. 59 lacs approximately. He stated that if L & T has to recover any amount from the sub contractor, it can be deducted from payments payable to him. He denied that it was responsibility of L & T to get the claimant treated for accidental injuries. He stated that there was an understanding that the cost of treatment shall be recovered from the payments payable to the sub contractor and balance amount towards cost of treatment shall also be deducted from the payments payable to the sub contractor. 18. In cross examination he again stated that there is no written contract containing a clause that expenses incurred by L & T on the treatment of employee of the sub contractor shall be recovered from the payments payable to the sub contractor. He stated that there is no other agreement between L & T and sub contractor except work order and there is no agreement that L & T will provide safety equipments to the employees of sub contractor. He admitted that it is not mentioned on the Worker's Bill that deduction of Rs. 2 lacs is towards cost of treatment of the claimant. He denied a suggestion that it was the duty of L & T to get the employees of sub contractor treated for injuries suffered at the site. Other suggestions contrary to his examination in chief were also denied by him. 19. Last witness examined by the claimant was Sh. Rakesh Kumar, Medical Record Officer as PW4 who produced discharge summary of claimant at Indian Spinal Injuries Centre which was exhibited as Ex. PW4/1. 20. On behalf of insurance company two witnesses were examined. The first witness that was examined was Sh. Harbhajan Singh, Assistant of M/s. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. as R3W1. He stated in his evidence by way of affidavit that the driving license of Respondent No. 1 was got Present Address vs Sh. Mahinder Kumar (Driver) on 29 October, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180513475/ 4 verified and a report was received from the Investigator that the driving license is fake. He stated that a notice was sent to the driver as well as owner of the vehicle to produce a valid driving license of the driver of the vehicle. He stated that although the insured was served with the notice but driver was not served with the notice as notice sent to him came back undelivered with the remarks that address is incomplete. He stated that insured had allowed the driver to drive the vehicle without a valid driving license and inspite of notice insured has not produced valid driving license of the driver and driver himself has not come to adduce any evidence or to produce his valid driving license. Therefore, this being a violation of terms and conditions of policy, the insurance company is not liable to indemnify the insured. 35. In Ranu Bala Paul & Ors. v. Bani Chakraborty & Ors. 1999 ACJ 634, the Hon'ble Gawhati High Court has observed as under: "In deciding a matter tribunal should bear in mind the caution struck by the Apex Court that a claim before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal is neither a criminal case nor a civil case. After all, it is a summary inquiry and this is a legislation for the welfare of the society" 36. In the case of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Vijay Laxmi & Ors. MAC APP. No. 375/06 dated 05.07.12, the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi has held as under: "8. In Bimla Devi and Ors. v. Present Address vs Sh. Mahinder Kumar (Driver) on 29 October, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180513475/ 6 Himachal Road Transport Corporation and Ors., (2009) 13 SC 530, the Supreme Court held that in a petition under Section 166 of the Act, the Claimants were merely to establish their case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability and holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition under the Motor Vehicles Act. Para 15 of the report is extracted hereunder: "15. In a situation of this nature, the Tribunal has rightly taken a holistic view of the matter. It was to be borne in mind that strict proof of an accident caused by a particular bus in a particular manner may not be possible to be done by the claimants. The claimants were merely to establish their case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability. The standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt could not have been applied." 9. The report in Bimla Devi (Supra) was relied on by the Supreme Court in its latest judgments in Parmeshwari v. Amir Chand (2011) 11 SCC 635 and Kusum Lata v. Satbir, (2011) 3 SCC 646." 37. In the case of National Insurance Company Ltd. v. Pushpa Rana & Ors.: 2009 ACJ 287, the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi has held that: "The last contention of the appellant insurance company is that the respondentsclaimants should have proved negligence on the part of the driver and in this regard the counsel has placed reliance on the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Meena Variyal (Supra). On perusal of the award of the Tribunal, it becomes clear that the wife of the deceased had produced: (i) certified copy of the criminal record of criminal case in F.I.R No. 955 of 2004, pertaining to involvement of the offending vehicle; (ii) criminal record showing completion of investigation of police and issue of chargesheet under Sections 279/304A, Indian Penal Code against the driver; (iii) certified copy of F.I.R., wherein criminal case against the driver was lodged; and (iv) recovery memo and mechanical inspection report of offending vehicle and vehicle of the deceased. These documents are sufficient proofs to reach the conclusion that the driver was negligent. Proceedings under the Motor Vehicles Act are not akin to proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not required to be followed in this regard. There is ample evidence on record to prove negligence on the part of the driver." 38. This case was noticed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case titled as Cholamandalam M.S. General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Kamlesh: 2009 (3) AD (Delhi) 310 where adverse inference was drawn because the driver of the offending vehicle had not appeared in the witness box to corroborate his defence taken in the written statement. It was noted that there is nothing on record to show that the claimant had any enmity with the driver of offending vehicle so as to falsely implicate him in the case. ISSUE NO. 2: 40. In the case of Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & Anr. ACJ 2011 (Vol. I), following principles were laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court for determining compensation payable to road traffic accident victims: Present Address vs Sh. Mahinder Kumar (Driver) on 29 October, 2013 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180513475/ 7 (i) The compensation payable to the claimant who is a victim of road accident should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident. The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equatable manner. (ii) Compensation payable in injury cases is payable under two heads. For this, reliance can be placed on Govind Goyenka v. Dayawati & Ors., which is a judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in FAO No. 81/2010 dated 21.03.12. 50.
